blocks.text: 几十年来，合理使用在推动惠及所有人的创新方面发挥了关键作用。它促成了重要的医学和科学突破，也催生了新技术，为无数人——包括作者和记者——带来了实实在在的积极改变。与此同时，《纽约时报》的诉讼却要求所有人无视半个世纪的法律历史与进步，为了自己狭隘的一己之利——一笔本不该得的赔偿——抛弃合理使用这一由来已久的原则。

blocks.text: 法院应当驳回原告试图将版权延伸至既定边界之外的请求。AI 训练对受版权保护作品的使用目的截然不同，不会向公众提供这些作品的替代性获取途径，也不会造成《版权法》所认定的市场损害。相反，它催生了一系列广泛的变革性技术，这些技术已经在带来公共利益。版权的存在是为了促进创造力和进步，而不是压制合法创新，也不是保护作者免受竞争。因此，既定的合理使用原则必然得出这样的结论：生成式 AI 训练属于合理使用。

blocks.text: 市场稀释理论要求版权法保护权利人免受一种它此前从未限制过的经济现象的影响。新作品可能降低旧作品的销量、曝光度或价值，却并未复制其受保护的表达。《版权法》有意将这种竞争置于版权人的控制之外。因此，法庭之友恳请法院裁定：“市场稀释”，即来自非侵权输出的总体竞争压力——包括那些占据相同主题或体裁、具有相同不受保护特征或争夺相同受众的输出——不属于《美国法典》第17编第107条第4款意义上的可认知市场损害。驳回该理论将维护第二巡回法院一贯坚持的区分：版权保护作者免受对其受保护表达的替代，而非免受仅仅与之竞争的新表达的成功。

blocks.text: AI 是一项变革性技术，能加速艺术与科学无数学科中新作品的创作。Kelly 先生对 AI 如何推动文学领域发展有切身体会。在他看来，每个 AI 模型都可以理解为一个全新的媒介，让作者有能力创作新的文本和思想，并进行推理。因此，若在合理使用问题上判原告胜诉，给予原告的将远远超出国会意图赋予其原创表达的有限垄断权。这会阻碍能够传播前所未有海量信息的技术的发展，也会妨碍新的思维模式以及艺术与科学领域新原创作品的创作。法庭之友提交本意见书，支持被告的论点，即为训练大语言模型而使用受版权保护的作品属于 17 U.S.C. § 107 下的合理使用。基于他毕生从事写作的经历，版权所有者获得的保护对 Kelly 先生很重要。同样至关重要的是，为版权材料的允许使用和变革性技术的发展保留空间。否则，版权将扼杀它本应鼓励的创造力、创新和知识传播。合理使用原则对于确保这种平衡至关重要。

blocks.text: 本意见书通过两位独立创作者的亲身经历，让人一窥这句话在实践中的含义——他们既依赖版权保护，也依赖 AI 工具来维持生计。法庭之友 Sarah Rose Siskind 和 Michael Wall 是创作并授权原创作品的艺术家。但他们用 AI 处理创作过程周边的工作，并在一个充斥着资源更雄厚竞争者的市场中发展自己的事业。对法庭之友而言，AI 并未取代创造力，也没有让他们走创作捷径。AI 帮助他们创作更多作品，并将作品延伸到新的表达形式。法庭之友的经历印证了美国的观点：AI 工具“能够也应该有助于拉平主流出版商与独立出版商之间的竞争环境”。Siskind 在业务的方方面面都用 AI，从日常行政事务到构思创意、招揽新客户。有了 AI，她的非创作工作更快、成本更低，创作工作也更好。用她的话说：“我觉得现在没有 AI，我的生意根本做不下去。”同样，AI 帮助 Wall 管理音乐业务的运营需求、降低成本，让他把更多时间投入作曲。和 Siskind 一样，他也怀疑没有 AI，自己的生意能否以目前的形式存续。

Cir. 2023)。合理使用同样有助于确保 AI 的益处惠及广大公众，而不是被少数特权者所掌控。

blocks.text: 在本案诉讼中，《纽约时报》试图限缩合理使用原则，将 OpenAI 大语言模型（LLM）的训练排除在外。这一结果将与版权法的基本原则相悖，并严重阻碍“科学与实用技艺的进步”。美国宪法第一条第 8 款第 8 项。如下文所述，包括独立媒体和初创媒体以及《纽约时报》本身在内的各类出版物，都在利用大语言模型服务于新闻及其他用途。而且，在本案争议标的之外，大语言模型已经在帮助各领域的研究人员取得重大突破。在误解合理使用原则的基础上限制大语言模型的发展，将阻碍此类创造性和科学进步，同时损害美国的繁荣与经济流动性。

blocks.text: For decades, fair use has played a critical role in driving innovation that benefits everyone. It has helped deliver important medical and scientific breakthroughs and new technologies that have made real and positive differences for countless people, including authors and journalists. The New York Times’ lawsuit, meanwhile, asks everyone to ignore a half century of legal history and progress, and toss aside the longstanding principle of fair use in their own narrow pursuit of an undeserved payday.

blocks.text: The Court should reject Plaintiffs’ attempt to extend copyright beyond its established limits. AI training uses copyrighted works for a fundamentally different purpose, does not provide the public with substitute access to those works, and does not cause the market harm cognizable under the Copyright Act. Instead, it enables a broad array of transformative technologies that are already delivering public benefits. Copyright exists to promote creativity and progress, not to suppress lawful innovation or protect authors from competition. Settled fair use principles therefore compel the conclusion that generative AI training is fair use.

blocks.text: This case concerns more than companies that develop large language models (LLMs). It affects medical researchers and patients, educators serving students with different learning needs, people with disabilities seeking greater independence, farmers applying agricultural knowledge, independent creators developing new forms of expression, and industry sectors from software to the law. These communities share an interest in the ability to study and learn from broad and diverse sources of knowledge, and in access to the tools that make that learning useful. Many depend on systems developed by others, including open source AI systems, rather than training models themselves. Fair use supports their ability to learn, discover, communicate, and create. Restrictions on fair use training would affect both the institutions building AI and the people using it.

blocks.text: The market dilution theory asks copyright law to protect rightsholders against an economic phenomenon that it has never restricted before. New works can reduce the sales, visibility, or value of older works without copying their protected expression. The Copyright Act deliberately leaves that competition outside the copyright owner’s control. Amicus therefore respectfully asks the Court to hold that “market dilution,” i.e., aggregate competitive pressure from noninfringing outputs, including those that occupy the same subject matter or genre, that share unprotected characteristics, or compete for the same audience, is not cognizable market harm under 17 U.S.C. § 107(4). Rejecting the theory would preserve the distinction the Second Circuit has always maintained: copyright protects authors against substitution for their protected expression, not against the success of new expression that merely competes with it.

blocks.text: Startups’ use of foundation models demonstrates that using copyrighted works to train an AI model is a fair use, not copyright infringement. The purpose of training a foundation model is not to reproduce the works it learns; it is to build a general-purpose tool that others can adapt to new ends. The ends startups have chosen bear no resemblance to the purposes of the works in any training dataset.

blocks.text: AI is a transformative technology that accelerates the creation of novel works across countless disciplines in the arts and sciences. Mr. Kelly has experience in how AI advances the field of literature. In his view, each AI model can be understood as an entirely new medium that offers authors the capability to create new texts and ideas, and to reason. A ruling for Plaintiffs on fair use would therefore grant Plaintiffs far more than the limited monopoly to their original expression Congress intended to confer. It would hinder the development of technologies capable of disseminating previously unimaginable quantities of information. It would also impede new modes of thought and the creation of new original works in both the arts and sciences. Amicus files this brief in support of Defendants’ argument that the use of copyrighted works to train large language models is a fair use under 17 U.S.C. § 107. Based on his lifelong pursuits of writing, the protections afforded to copyright owners are important to Mr. Kelly. Equally vital is preserving room for permissible uses of copyrighted material and the growth of transformative technologies. Otherwise, copyright will stifle the very creativity, innovation, and spread of knowledge it exists to encourage. The fair-use doctrine is critical to ensuring that balance.

blocks.text: This brief offers a window into what that sentence means in practice through the work of two independent creators who rely on copyright protection and AI tools to sustain their livelihoods. Amici Sarah Rose Siskind and Michael Wall are artists who create and license original works. But they use AI to handle work surrounding the creative process and to grow their businesses in a market teeming with better-resourced competitors. For Amici, AI does not displace creativity or shortcut their creative processes. AI helps them create more, and to extend their work into new modes of expression. Amici’s experience underscores the United States’ view that AI tools “can and should help level the playing field between mainstream and independent publishers.” Siskind uses AI in every aspect of her business, from day-to-day administrative tasks to developing ideas and bringing in new clients. With AI, her noncreative work is faster and less expensive, and her creative work is better. As she tells it, “I don’t think I could run my business without AI at this point.” Similarly, AI helps Wall manage the operational demands of his music business, reduce costs, and devote more of his time to composing music. Like Siskind, he doubts that his business could survive in its current form without AI.

blocks.text: Fair use has protected tools that help people navigate the vast collections of information the digital world has brought us, including image search and full-text book search. See Perfect 10, Inc. v. Amazon.com, Inc., 508 F.3d 1146, 1164–68 (9th Cir. 2007); Authors Guild v. Google, Inc., 804 F.3d 202, 216–17, 225 (2d Cir. 2015) (“Google Books”). It has also protected libraries’ provision of accessible digital books to readers with print disabilities. See Authors Guild, Inc. v. HathiTrust, 755 F.3d 87, 101–03 (2d Cir. 2014). And it has protected free online publication of technical standards incorporated into law, recognizing the “substantial public benefits of free and easy access to the law.” Am. Soc’y for Testing & Materials v. Public.Resource.Org, Inc., 82 F.4th 1262, 1271–72 (D.C. Cir. 2023). Fair use will be equally beneficial in ensuring that AI’s benefits accrue to the public at large, instead of being controlled by a privileged few.

blocks.text: OpenAI’s use of newspaper articles to train its generative AI models didn’t harm the reasonable commercial expectations of the News Plaintiffs in any way. They commissioned and published newspaper articles with the expectation of selling consumers access to those articles. They retain and continue to exercise the exclusive right to sell consumers access to their articles. Their ability to sell consumers access to their articles wasn’t affected by OpenAI’s use of those articles to train its AI models.

blocks.text: In this litigation, the New York Times seeks to narrow fair-use doctrine to exclude the training of OpenAI’s large language models (LLMs). That result would be inconsistent with basic copyright law principles and severely hamper “the Progress of Science and useful Arts.” U.S. CONST. art. I, § 8, cl. 8. As discussed below, publications—including independent and start-up media, in addition to the New York Times itself—are leveraging LLMs for journalistic and other purposes. And beyond the subject matter of this litigation, LLMs are already helping researchers across fields achieve major breakthroughs. Constraining LLM development under a misunderstanding of fair use doctrine would thwart such creative and scientific progress while hindering American prosperity and economic mobility.
